papers.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
papers.abstract: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $\alpha$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.

papers.title: Location-Aware Matching Statistics
papers.abstract: Edit distance is the standard measure of string similarity, but its quadratic-time complexity is prohibitive for long strings. Popular linear-time alternatives, such as the $q$-gram distance, or the average common substring measure (ACS) that is based on matching statistics (MS), consider the substrings shared by the two input strings but not where they occur in each string. Yet in many real-world applications, e.g., when comparing document versions or co-recorded time series, a shared substring is really relevant only if its occurrences are close in position. We introduce Location-Aware Matching Statistics (LAMAS). Given strings $X$ and $Y$ and a displacement tolerance $d$, LAMAS reports, for every position $i$ of $Y$, the longest substring starting at $i$ that occurs in $X$ at a position $j$ with $|j-i|\le d$, together with the displacement $(j-i)$. MS is the special case of LAMAS with unbounded $d$. Our main result is an algorithm that solves LAMAS in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time and space for strings of length at most $n$ and any $d$; this is optimal and matches the complexity of MS. The algorithm reduces LAMAS to predecessor and successor queries over a sliding window of suffix ranks and answers them in linear total time via a window decomposition and interval union-find. Experiments on 20 real datasets and synthetic data show that LAMAS substantially improves over MS and $q$-gram distance in similarity-based classification, top-$K$ retrieval, and clustering. It is competitive with edit distance and a constrained dynamic time warping variant in classification and generally outperforms a state-of-the-art method for top-$K$ retrieval under edit distance. Finally, our implementation of the main algorithm for LAMAS scales linearly in $n$ and does not slow down as $d$ grows.

papers.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
papers.abstract: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.

papers.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.

papers.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
papers.abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We survey bounds that can be recovered from earlier work under FPT $\neq$ W[1] and prove seven lower bounds for graph problems and set systems under the same assumption. The new proofs encode clique choices in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of the encoding. This lets us turn a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem into a fixed-parameter algorithm for Clique or Multicolored Clique. In several cases, the new bound matches the function of the parameter in the historical exponent, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.

papers.title: Cliques, Quasi-Cliques, and Bicliques in Random Graphs: Sampling and Algorithms
papers.abstract: We study the algorithmic problem of finding dense subgraphs - cliques, quasi-cliques, and bicliques - in Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs. While the extremal structure of cliques in $G(n,1/2)$ is well understood, efficiently locating large cliques remains a central algorithmic challenge. We introduce a new perspective on this problem: the classical Grimmett-McDiarmid greedy algorithm implicitly defines a near-uniform sampler over cliques of size $(1-o(1))\log n$. Building on this observation, we develop a sampling-based framework for finding larger cliques. In particular, for every $\eta>0$, we give an algorithm that finds a clique of size $(1+\eta)\log n$ in time $n^{(\eta^2/2+o(1))\log n}$ - the first smooth trade-off between clique size and running time in this regime, improving on the previously best-known running time of $n^{(1/2+o(1))\log n}$. We further show that improved sampling algorithms for cliques of size $(1+\eta)\log n$ translate into faster algorithms for finding a maximum clique. Beyond cliques, we give a deterministic algorithm that enumerates all maximum $\gamma$-quasi-cliques in $G(n,p)$ in time matching their count up to lower-order factors, and extend this to random bipartite graphs $G(n,n,p)$, establishing new concentration bounds for quasi-bicliques together with analogous enumeration algorithms. Finally, we study unbalanced bicliques in $G(n,n,p)$. For each $s \in [n]$, we obtain a concentration bound on the largest $t = t_{\max}(s)$ for which an $(s,t)$-biclique exists, and show that when $s = \omega(\log n)$, a simple greedy algorithm finds an $(s,(1-o(1))t_{\max}(s))$-biclique in linear time with high probability - demonstrating that greedy is near-optimal in this regime.

papers.title: A $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for Weighted 3-Set Packing
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted $3$-set packing, for every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, improving on the 1.6908-approximation reported by Tong and Xu (2026). The algorithm has two phases. It first performs bounded local search using a rounded $12/7$-power potential. It then combines compatible exchanges that insert at most three sets and increase the original weight. The analysis relates the gap left by the first phase to the gain available to the second phase. We prove a structural inequality that bounds the weight of a comparison packing by $3/2$ times the current weight plus one sixth of a sum of small-exchange gains. Each gain accounts for all sets that the exchange must delete. A greedy rule recovers enough of these gains to obtain the approximation guarantee. We derive the structural bound from local optimality by analyzing finite computation trees and averaging the error caused by their limited depth. The running time is $n^{4^{O(1/\varepsilon)}}\operatorname{poly}(L)$, where $n$ is the number of input sets and $L$ is the input encoding length. The same guarantee holds for maximum-weight independent set in induced $K_{1,4}$-free graphs.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Rank Estimation in Turnstile Streams
papers.abstract: We study rank estimation in turnstile streams. A frequency vector $f$ over the universe $[U]$ receives insertions and deletions. Given a query $x\in[U]$, the goal is to estimate the rank $\sum_{u<x}f_u$ within additive error $\epsilon\|f\|_1$ with constant probability. The standard approach is Dyadic CountSketch by Luo, Wang, Yi and Cormode, using $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U\log n)$ bits, where $n$ is the final $\ell_1$ norm of $f$. Bul\'anek, Kumar, Meka, Nelson, and Sarl\'os placed this approach in a matrix-factorization framework. They improved the space of Dyadic CountSketch to $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U)$ words, and proved a lower bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}\log^2(\epsilon U))$ bits for all streaming algorithms when $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$. This leaves a gap of $\sqrt{\log U}$. In this work, we fully determine the space cost of rank estimation up to an absolute constant. Our main result is a space lower bound for all streaming algorithms: for $0<\epsilon\le 1/8$ and $n\ge\log^2 U$, the space is at least $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}L^{3/2}\log(2+n\epsilon/\sqrt{L}), \epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n, \log\binom{U+n}{n}\})$ bits, where $L=\log(2+U\epsilon)$. When $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$, this simplifies to $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}\log^{5/2}U, \epsilon^{-2}\log^2 U\})$ bits. Our proof uses a surprising hard distribution and novel information-theoretic techniques. The above bound matches Dyadic CountSketch when $n\ge U$ and $U^{-1+\Omega(1)}\le\epsilon\le O(1/\sqrt{\log U})$. The lower bound is also tight in the remaining regimes. For $\epsilon\ge(\log U)^{-1/2}$, there exists an algorithm that uses $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n)$ bits using $\ell_1$ samplers. For $\epsilon\le U^{-1+o(1)}$, we refine Dyadic CountSketch so that its space in bits matches the first term of the bound.

papers.title: String Indexing for Maximal Gap-Bounded Occurrence Clusters
papers.abstract: Repeated occurrences of a pattern can form groups that reveal where repetition is concentrated in a text. We study how to find such groups efficiently when both the pattern $P$ and the distance threshold $G$ between occurrences are specified as query parameters. A maximal $G$-cluster of $P$ is a maximal block of at least two occurrences of $P$ whose consecutive starting positions differ by at most $G$. In this paper, we present indexes for reporting all cluster intervals and counting the clusters. For a text of length $n$ and a pattern of length $m$, we propose an $O(n\log n)$-space index that reports all maximal cluster intervals in $O(m+\log\log n+\mathit{output})$ time, where $\mathit{output}$ is the number of reported intervals, and that counts the clusters in $O(m+\log\log n)$ time. Restricting occurrences to those fully contained in a query substring preserves the reporting time using $O(n\log^2 n)$ space. Our indexes combine suffix-tree decompositions with geometric reporting queries on consecutive gaps.

papers.title: Towards a faster parameterized algorithm for Chordal Vertex Deletion
papers.abstract: The \textsc{Chordal Vertex Deletion} (\chvd{}) problem asks whether an input graph $G$ can be made chordal by removing at most $k$ vertices. When $k$ is taken as parameter, this problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable \cite{M10,CM16}. However, it is still open whether \chvd{} admits a single-exponential FPT algorithm, i.e. an algorithm with running time $O(\alpha^k |V(G)|^c)$ for some constant $\alpha$ independent of $k$. Towards this goal, we describe an FPT algorithm for the compression version of \chvd{} with the following specification. Given an instance $I = (G,k,X)$ of the disjoint \chvd{} compression problem such that $|X| = k+1$, $G - X$ is chordal and its longest chordless path has length $L$, we solve $I$ in time $O((L+1)^{3k} k^2 |V(G)|^4)$.

papers.title: Exact edge cover by strict and non-strict temporal walks
papers.abstract: Exact edge cover asks whether the edges of a temporal graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges can be partitioned into time-respecting walks with a prescribed number of walks starting at each vertex and, in the fixed-end variant, ending at each vertex. For non-strict walks, we prove that the problem is polynomially solvable by a new approach based on M-convexity, which also closes a gap in the proof sketch of an earlier static reduction. An orientation of the edges is realizable by walks exactly when walk counters stay non-negative and every snapshot component contains a walk, and only components with all degrees and counters even can violate the latter condition. Once a dead state is removed, the states of each such component form an M-convex set. This yields an augmenting path algorithm that returns walks or an infeasibility certificate, using at most $m/2$ augmentations and $O(n+nm^2)$ arithmetic operations with path-reversing re-orientation. The implementation was validated on small instances. For strict walks, we prove that the problem is NP-complete, already with six time labels for prescribed ends and two for free ends.

papers.title: A Simple Optimal Algorithm for Directed Multi-Failure Replacement Paths
papers.abstract: Given a graph $G = (V, E)$ and two vertices $s, t \in V$, the $f$-fault replacement paths ($f$-FRP) problem asks to compute, for every set $F$ of at most $f$ edges, the distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G \setminus F$. In this paper, we present a $3$-FRP algorithm in deterministic $O(n^3 \log n)$ time for directed weighted graphs. We also present a deterministic $O(n^4)$ time algorithm for $4$-FRP in directed weighted graphs, which implies a deterministic $O(n^f)$ time algorithm for $f$-FRP for every $f \ge 4$. Since the output size of $f$-FRP can be $\Theta(n^f)$, our algorithms are optimal for every $f \ge 4$ and nearly optimal for $f = 3$. Our algorithms also extend to the single-source and all-pairs settings with $f-1$ and $f-2$ failures, respectively, with the same time complexity as $f$-FRP. Moreover, our algorithms are remarkably simple.

papers.title: Algorithms for Collaborative Truck-Multi-Drone Delivery in the En-Route Model
papers.abstract: We study collaborative truck--multi-drone delivery in the en-route model, in which a truck moves continuously along a fixed straight-line path while drones serve $n$ off-route deliveries. For maximum coverage with $k$ drones, we prove that Sequential Greedy achieves an approximation guarantee of $1-(k/(k+1))^k$, which approaches $1-e^{-1}$. For $k=2$, our analysis is tight, with a matching $5/9$ instance. We refute the claimed exchange property for proper instances. For a new class of swap-monotone instances with distinct $x$-coordinates, we give an exact $O(n^2)$-time dynamic program for single-drone maximum coverage. For minimum fleet size, we prove NP-hardness and give an $O(1+\log(n/k^\ast))$-approximation using an integer residual bound, where $k^\ast$ is the optimum fleet size.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Orientable Domination
papers.abstract: The orientable domination number of an undirected graph $G$ is the maximum over all orientations $D$ of $G$ of the minimum size of a dominating set of $D$. In this paper, we look at the problem to decide if the orientable domination number of a given undirected graph $G$ is at least a given integer $\ell$. We show that this problem is complete for the class $\Sigma_2^P$, is fixed-parameter tractable by treewidth, and has a polynomial kernel parameterized by vertex cover number.

papers.title: A Local-to-Global Approximation Framework for Covering Disjointness-Compliable Set Families
papers.abstract: Many network design problems can be formulated as covering a family of vertex sets by edges. We develop a local-to-global approximation framework for disjointness-compliable families with polynomial-time membership tests. A class of vertices is deficient if it belongs to the family and feasible otherwise. Our local problem seeks a minimum-cost tree that connects one deficient class to feasible classes so that their union is feasible. If this local problem admits a polynomial-time $\alpha$-approximation, then the covering problem admits a polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{\alpha})^2$-approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Our algorithm first connects deficient vertices that are difficult to separate and then handles regions containing one deficient class at a time. To bound the total local cost, we compare the local trees with a feasible forest. We delete edges of this forest after using them in the bound, so each is counted at most once even when regions overlap. As applications, we obtain polynomial-time $(8+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for generalized point-to-point connection and multiroot quota tree, including multiroot $k$-minimum spanning tree. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-time constant-factor approximations for both problems. We also obtain a randomized approximation for multiroot covering Steiner that has the same asymptotic ratio as the known approximation for its single-root version.

papers.title: Exponential memory/query-complexity tradeoffs in high-accuracy feasibility problems
papers.abstract: We prove memory/query-complexity tradeoff lower bounds for the feasibility problem, where the goal is to find a point within an $\epsilon$-ball hidden in the unit $d$-dimensional ball, with access to a separation oracle. This problem admits three regimes: the low-accuracy regime $\epsilon\geq 1/\sqrt d$ where memory does not play a role, the medium-accuracy regime $1/\sqrt d\geq \epsilon\geq e^{-\Omega(d\ln d)}$ where prior works identified strong memory/query-complexity separations, and the high-accuracy regime $\epsilon\leq e^{-\Omega(d\ln d)}$ for which much less is known. In this regime, low-memory algorithms with significantly faster convergence rates than gradient descent have been developed in [BZJ24]: for accuracy $\epsilon$ and any $\delta\in[0,1]$, these require $d^{1+\delta}\ln \frac1\epsilon$ memory bits and use $\left(d\ln\frac1{\epsilon}\right)^{O(d^{1-\delta})}$ oracle queries. In comparison, gradient descent uses the same memory for $\delta=0$ but requires $1/\epsilon^2$ oracle queries. On the lower-bound side, no non-trivial memory/query-complexity tradeoff was known: the best lower bound remained the historical memory-independent bound $\Omega(d\ln \frac1\epsilon)$ from [NYD83]. We make progress towards characterizing the memory landscape in this high-accuracy regime by showing that for any $\delta\in[0,1]$, any algorithm with $d^{1+\delta}\ln\frac1{\epsilon}$ bits of memory uses at least $\left(d\ln\frac1{\epsilon}\right)^{\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{(1-\delta)/8})}$ oracle calls. This result justifies the seemingly peculiar exponential-in-$d$ dependence of oracle complexity for the aforementioned low-memory algorithms. In particular, our result shows that for high-accuracy feasibility problems, insufficient memory does result in an exponential price in the dimension for the query-complexity.

papers.title: Randomized MST Certification beyond Cacti
papers.abstract: We study minimum spanning tree certification under explorable edge uncertainty. Edge weights lie in open intervals or singleton sets, and querying an edge reveals its weight at a known positive cost. On general graphs the best known randomized competitive ratio is $1+1/\sqrt2$, while the optimal ratio $3/2$ is known only for cacti. We go beyond cacti in two ways, with conditions that refer to the uncertain edges outside the upper-limit tree rather than to the graph alone. For unit query costs we give a $3/2$-competitive algorithm, which is best possible, whenever every block has at most two such edges; this includes all graphs whose blocks are cycles or theta graphs. The algorithm replaces the constant budget of the water-filling method by budgets chosen with lookahead to the next fundamental cycle. For arbitrary positive query costs and every fixed $k\ge1$, we obtain ratio $1+\sqrt{k/(2(k+1))}$ whenever every block has at most $k$ such edges, in particular when every block has cycle rank at most $k$. This is below $1+1/\sqrt2$ for every $k$, and we show that it is the best ratio attainable with a constant water-filling budget.

papers.title: Asymptotically Optimal Representation of Tree-Like Graphs
papers.abstract: We show how to represent a graph with $n$ nodes, $m=n+k=O(n)$ edges, and $h\le k$ nodes with more than one incoming edge in asymptotically optimal space, in a way that supports basic navigational operations quickly.

papers.title: Faster Directed SSSP on Digraphs with Random Sparse Supports or Few DFS Exceptions
papers.abstract: We study exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs and nonnegative real weights, in the comparison-addition model. This paper continues our earlier work, which gave a deterministic algorithm that takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$ time when $m=O(n)$ and $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$ time when $m=\Theta(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$. Our two deterministic algorithms compute the distances on every input and take $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time on two families of inputs, one per density. The support of an input is its underlying simple undirected graph. When $m=O(n)$, the first algorithm takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time if no two simple cycles of the support with fewer than $P$ vertices share a vertex, where $P=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ depends only on the support. For fixed $c>0$, a uniformly random graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ edges has this property with probability at least $1-n^{-1+o(1)}$, and the bound then holds for every choice of one or both directions of each edge, all weights and every source. The second family is defined through the depth-first search tree of the support that starts at the source and visits neighbours in identifier order. For fixed $k\ge1$, call a set $Y$ of exceptional vertices $k$-feasible if, for each nonroot vertex, at most $k$ of its proper ancestors are joined to its subtree by arcs whose endpoints avoid $Y$ and whose underlying edges lie outside the DFS tree. Given $k$ but not such a set, the second algorithm takes, for every $k$-feasible set $Y$ of total out-degree $d^+(Y)$, time $O_k(n+m+(1+|Y|)\log n+\sqrt{(n+m)d^+(Y)\log n})$. When $m=\Theta(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, this is $O_k(n\sqrt{\log n})$ if some $k$-feasible set has $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ vertices and total out-degree $O(n/\sqrt{\log\log n})$.

papers.title: An $n^{1/O(\log^* n)}$ Lower Bound for Online Coloring of $k$-Colorable Graphs
papers.abstract: In online coloring, the vertices of a graph arrive one at a time with their edges to earlier vertices, and each vertex must be colored irrevocably on arrival. For graphs promised to be $k$-colorable, with $k\ge 3$ fixed, the best deterministic algorithms use $n^{1-\Theta(1/k^2)}$ colors, while the best lower bound was Vishwanathan's $\Omega(\log^{k-1}n)$ from 1990 until Li recently proved $2^{\Omega((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})}$. For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we prove a lower bound of $n^{1/(\log^*n+3)}$ colors for deterministic online algorithms on $n$-vertex $k$-colorable graphs, and the same lower bound in expectation for randomized online algorithms. Both bounds hold on a single triangle-free $3$-colorable graph: even an algorithm that is shown this graph in advance, but is not told which of its vertices each arriving vertex is, can be forced to use this many colors by a suitable arrival order. The hard instances are iterated blow-ups of a clique, in which every vertex becomes a block of independent vertices and every edge a private server in the earlier block; each blow-up keeps the forced colors and replaces the chromatic number $\chi$ by about $\log\chi$, so about $\log^*n$ blow-ups bring it down to $k$. We also show that deterministic lower bounds for different values of $k\ge 3$ are polynomially equivalent, and that no adversary presenting such iterated blow-ups can force more than $n^{1/(\log^*n-O(1))}$ colors. All numbered results are formalized in Lean 4.

papers.title: Improved Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Path TSP and Ordered TSP
papers.abstract: In Multi-Path TSP, given a metric and $k$ pairs of vertices $(s_i,t_i)$, where $k$ is part of the input, we seek $s_i$--$t_i$ paths of minimum total length that together visit all vertices. Ratios below $2$ were known only for graphic metrics and special cases such as multiple depots ($s_i=t_i$); in general metrics, the best ratio was $1+2e^{-1/2}\approx2.213$, by a randomized algorithm of B\"ohm, Friggstad, M\"omke and Spoerhase [SODA 2025]. We give a deterministic algorithm with ratio $\frac{5e-2}{3e-2}<1.8833$ relative to a restriction of their LP relaxation, bounding its integrality gap by the same constant. For Ordered TSP, where a tour must visit $k$ given vertices in a prescribed cyclic order, we compute tours within $1+\frac{e}{2(e-1)}<1.7910$ times the value of the LP relaxation of Armbruster, Mnich and N\"agele [APPROX 2024], improving $\frac32+\frac1e\approx1.868$ on both the ratio and the integrality gap. Our algorithms sample a tree for every pair (for Ordered TSP, every two consecutive given vertices) from an LP solution, but keep only the path between the two endpoints. Our main lemma shows that, for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights, a cheapest forest connecting all vertices to these paths has expected weight at most $1/e$ times that of a cheapest forest rooted at the endpoints plus $(1-1/e)$ times the expected weight of the discarded branches. For Multi-Path TSP, we use the weights of a primal--dual growth process that Zhao, Liu and Xiao [arXiv 2026] designed for multiple depots; in these weights, the connecting forest also pays for part of correcting its degree parities.

papers.title: Tight Query Depth of Recursive Randomized Greedy MIS
papers.abstract: The randomized greedy maximal independent set (RGMIS) algorithm processes vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily constructs an MIS. Its recursive formulation decides whether a vertex belongs to this MIS by querying lower-ranked neighbors in increasing rank order, stopping when a neighbor in the MIS is found. We prove that, on every $n$-vertex graph, this recursive algorithm has $O(\log n)$ query depth with high probability, even without memoization. The bound holds simultaneously for all starting vertices and is asymptotically tight even on bipartite graphs. The proof combines a bound on the total expected number of query paths with an exposure argument: paths with many two-edge shortcuts are unlikely, while the remaining paths admit sufficiently many applications of a two-hop probability bound.

papers.title: Trusted Advice for Scheduling on Unrelated Machines
papers.abstract: Scheduling on unrelated parallel machines under standard objectives, such as makespan minimization or max-min fairness, has posed fundamental theoretical challenges for decades. A prominent example is the longstanding factor 2 approximation barrier for the Min Makespan problem established by Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990). We investigate these fundamental challenges within the framework of algorithms with trusted advice. We consider a setting in which a trusted oracle is accessed once and reveals partial but entirely accurate structural information about an optimal solution. This framework allows us to quantify the improvements in approximation guarantees enabled by various trusted advice. We formalize a hierarchy of trusted advice oracles, ranging from a strong oracle that reveals the exact assignments of long jobs to a weaker oracle that indicates only which machines process such jobs. By exploiting this information, we obtain approximation guarantees beyond the classical worst-case barriers. In particular, we show that even the weakest oracle improves the approximation ratio for Min Makespan to $\sqrt{3}\approx 1.732$. We also obtain improved ratios of $(\sqrt{33}+1)/4\approx 1.686$ and $(5\sqrt{7})/8 \approx 1.654$ for Restricted Assignment and Graph Balancing, respectively. For the max-min fairness objective, known as the Santa Claus problem, we obtain a 2-approximation using our weak oracle. Finally, we show that these problems remain NP-hard to approximate within certain constant factors even with the trusted advice oracles considered. Interestingly, for the Santa Claus problem, we show a lower bound of 2 which is tight and matches the classical oracle-free bound.

papers.title: Constrained Online Selection with Predictions: Matroid Secretary, Knapsack, and Matching
papers.abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for constrained online selection problems, including the secretary problem under matroid and knapsack constraints, and the edge-weighted online bipartite matching problem with random vertex arrivals. In each, items arrive in a uniformly random order, and their values are revealed only on arrival. The goal is to select a set of items with nearly maximum total value, subject to the constraints (matroid, knapsack, or matching). In the learning-augmented setting, item value predictions are given in advance. We seek algorithms that are both consistent, in that accurate predictions lead to near-optimal selection, and robust, in that they obtain strong worst-case bounds even when predictions are inaccurate. Building on work of Fujii and Yoshida (2024) on the learning-augmented secretary problem, we study a method that follows the predicted optimum until an item with a large enough prediction error is observed. At that point, it reverts to running a worst-case competitive algorithm. We make a simple but critical modification: the first item with a large prediction error is selected with a carefully chosen probability. With this modification, we prove a general result, showing that if the underlying worst-case algorithm is $\alpha$-competitive for $\alpha\in(0,1]$, this approach achieves competitive ratio $\max\{\frac{\alpha}{2(1+\alpha)},\frac{1-\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\}$, where $\epsilon$ is the maximum relative error of any prediction. That is, the algorithm is perfectly consistent, achieving competitive ratio $1$ as $\epsilon \to 0$, and robust up to a constant factor relative to the worst-case baseline. For all three problems we study, $\alpha = 1/e$, and our result is the first to achieve consistency and constant-factor robustness. We hope that our general analysis framework can be applied to other learning-augmented online decision-making problems.

papers.title: A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

papers.title: Weighted Flow Time Does Not Admit Constant-Competitive Randomized Algorithms
papers.abstract: We study online preemptive scheduling on a single machine with the objective of minimizing the total weighted flow time. Bansal and Chan (SODA 2009) showed that no deterministic online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive for this problem. We show that no randomized online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary either. This settles the remaining case of the long-standing question whether the problem admits an $O(1)$-competitive online algorithm. Quantitatively, every randomized online algorithm has a competitive ratio in $\Omega(\min\{\log\log W,\log\log\log\min\{P,D,n\}\})$, where $n$ is the number of jobs and $W$, $P$, and $D$ are the ratios of the largest to the smallest job weight, size, and density (weight divided by size), respectively. The lower bound also holds with high probability, with the same asymptotic dependence on the instance parameters. For every $\rho\ge1$ and every randomized online algorithm, there is an instance on which the cost of the algorithm is at least $\rho$ times the optimal cost with probability at least $1-2^{-2^\rho}$. Both lower bounds hold even if the algorithm knows in advance the size and weight of every job in release order and, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every interarrival time up to a factor of $1+\varepsilon$.

papers.title: First-Order Entropic Sampling of Words with Prescribed Letter Counts in Linear Time
papers.abstract: We sample, exactly and uniformly, a word of length n over the alphabet {0, . . . , r} in which the letter j occurs a prescribed positive number k j of times, from a source of fair random bits. Every exact sampler reads on average at least H = log 2 (___ n k0,...,kr )___ bits. We give a sampler that reads on average at most H fresh bits, whatever r and the counts, and that performs O(n) bit operations on average over every fixed alphabet, in a bit-RAM in which a memory access costs O(1) while arithmetic is charged bit by bit. Both bounds are optimal: the first one to first order, the second one up to a constant factor, since writing the output already costs $\Theta$(n). The sampler writes the word as a Huffman tree of independent binary words, and samples each of them in one of two ways. Binary words with few ones are generated by random insertions; the rank of each inserted letter among its copies, which the Fisher-Yates shuffle generates for nothing, is uniform and independent of the word, and is given back to a recycling source of uniform integers, where it pays for the next insertions. Binary words with many ones are generated by MergeShuffle driven by blocks of $\Theta$(log n) bits of entropy; a block is decoded by locating only its ones when the minority letter is rare, and otherwise, its number of ones being concentrated, by a precomputed table of the blocks of typical type, of size O( $\sqrt$ n log 4 n), the rare atypical blocks being decoded slowly.

papers.title: Via a New LP Relaxation: Stronger Performance Guarantees for WSEPT, and an LP-Based Proof of Kawaguchi & Kyan
papers.abstract: We present a new linear programming relaxation for minimizing the total weighted completion time on identical parallel machines. Its right-hand side is supermodular, so the relaxation can be solved by a greedy algorithm. We show that the WSPT rule is within a factor $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{2})$ of the optimal LP value. This bounds the integrality gap of the relaxation and gives a short, LP-based proof of the tight bound of Kawaguchi and Kyan on the performance of WSPT. We then turn to the stochastic version of the problem, in which processing times are independent random variables whose squared coefficients of variation are at most~$\Delta$. A variance-corrected version of the new LP relaxation is valid for all non-anticipatory policies, and we show that WSEPT is within a factor $1 + (1 + \Delta)/(3 + \sqrt{7 + 2 \Delta})$ of it for $\Delta \ge 1$, for any number of machines. This is $O(\sqrt\Delta)$, whereas all previous guarantees for this problem grow linearly in $\Delta$. Up to a constant factor, our bound matches the known $\Omega(\sqrt\Delta)$ lower bound for WSEPT. For $\Delta \le 1$, we recover the best known bounds.

papers.title: Optimizing Diameter of r-Gather under Connectivity Constraints from Convex to Connected
papers.abstract: The $r$-gather problem partitions the nodes of an edge-weighted graph into clusters of at least $r$ nodes each. The problem is NP-hard, and known approximation algorithms may return clusters whose induced subgraphs are disconnected. We therefore require each cluster to be connected, or even convex in the existential sense that some shortest path between any two of its members stays inside the cluster. We add a parameterized $\alpha$-ratio-convex variant that interpolates between the two by bounding the induced stretch by a factor $\alpha$. We measure the cost of a clustering by its diameter, the largest pairwise distance within a cluster, rather than by the radius as in the classical formulation. We show that the variants form a hierarchy, that they remain NP-hard in general, and that none of them admits a polynomial-time $(2-\varepsilon)$-approximation unless P=NP. Our main algorithmic result is a polynomial-time algorithm for convex $r$-gather on trees. This contrasts with connected $k$-diameter, which remains hard even on star-like connectivity graphs. On general weighted graphs, we give a $4$-approximation for connected $r$-gather. Extending the tree algorithm to tree decompositions, we obtain an exact algorithm for connected $r$-gather that is fixed-parameter tractable in the treewidth together with $d$ and $r$. Finally, we relate the $\alpha$-ratio-convex variant to $t$-spanners, which yields further approximation guarantees.

papers.title: Tight Analysis for Online Generalized Network Design with Power Functions
papers.abstract: We study the online generalized network design problem with heterogeneous power costs. Here, a sequence of $N$ requests arrive online, each of which needs to be assigned to some subset of available resources $E$. Each resource $e\in E$ has its own coefficient $\xi_e>0$ and exponent $p_e\ge 1$, where the cost of a load vector $L\in \mathbb{R}^E_+$ is $\Phi(L)=\sum_{e\in E}\xi_e L_e^{p_e}$. We provide a simple analysis for the natural greedy algorithm that $\tau$-approximately minimizes the increase in $\Phi$ for each online request. Our competitive ratio is at most $(\frac{p}{\ln 2})^p$ when $\tau=1$ and is roughly $(\tau p)^p$ as $\tau$ grows large; here $p=\max_{e\in E} p_e$. This improves over a prior competitive ratio of $2(e\tau p)^p$ that relied on a modified greedy algorithm and a more complex analysis. Moreover, our bound (with $\tau=1$) is asymptotically optimal: it matches the $(1.443p)^p$ lower bound for deterministic online algorithms. We also provide a nuanced exponent-dependent bound that, combined with prior results, provides an improved competitive ratio for (dis)economies of scale cost functions; here, the cost of resource $e$ has the form $\sigma_e + \xi_e\cdot x^{p_e}$ if $x>0$ (and zero if $x=0$). These results apply to several fundamental network problems such as multicommodity routing (where $\tau=1$), Steiner tree connectivity (where $\tau=1.39$) and directed Steiner connectivity (where $\tau$ is poly-logarithmic).
